d.title: One call, and the tool output is the answer
d.caption: Worth naming as a rung because **“look this up” is a real and common requirement, and people reach for an agent loop to serve it.** The measurement is the argument: the model asked for `lookup_policy`, the tool returned the policy sentence, and that sentence **is** what the user wanted — so **returning it is the whole system**, and anything after it is a formatting decision rather than a capability.

nodes.label: The model asks for one tool
So returning it is the whole system

d.title: The branch does no model work, which is where the cheapness comes from
d.caption: `['classified as billing', 'billing handled it']` at **1 model call** — one classification, and the branch itself costs nothing. Which is what buys the two properties the rungs above give up: **the paths are enumerable because they are edges you wrote, and looping is not merely unlikely but structurally impossible**, because there is no edge back.

nodes.label: The branch does no model work

d.title: Two model calls for an answer the first tool call already had
d.caption: The list grows to four messages and the counter reads **2** — and **the second call exists only to turn the tool result into prose.** Sometimes that is exactly what you want, because structured data does need turning into a sentence. So the question at rung 4 is **whether you are buying the loop or the phrasing**: if it is the phrasing, you are at rung 2 with a formatting step, and formatting does not need to be a loop.

d.title: Does the sequence vary, or only the choice?
d.caption: If only the **choice** varies — the request is one of five kinds and each needs one known operation — **a conditional edge expresses it exactly**, and you are on rung 3. If the **sequence** genuinely varies, because the next action depends on what the last one returned in a way you cannot enumerate, you need rung 4. **That is the only honest justification for the loop**, and it is a claim about the task rather than about the framework.

nodes.label: A conditional edge says it exactly
Sequence: not enumerable
nodes.sub: next depends on the last result

d.title: Guessing low costs a branch; guessing high costs you the ability to say anything
d.caption: **A bounded pattern that nearly works is one branch away from working — the gap is visible and the fix is local.** An agent that works unpredictably is a measurement problem, a cost problem and a debugging problem **at once**, and none of those is one change away from fixed. Which is why the rule is *stop at the lowest rung that works* rather than *choose the appropriate rung*: the two errors are not the same size.

nodes.label: So: stop at the lowest rung that works

d.title: No amount of care in the router's code closes this
d.caption: 8.7's version was a router whose **own code** could return an unmapped key, fixable by enumerating the outcomes with an `Enum` and building the map from them. **Here the value comes from a model, and the set of strings a model can emit is not enumerable** — each row below is a different unmapped key, and a refusal is a fifth. Which is why the ceiling of the pattern is set by this one failure.

d.title: Structured output moves the failure to a better place, and does not remove it
d.caption: Constraining the generation changes the failure from *“the model said something else”* to *“the provider rejected the generation”* — **loud, and at the boundary**, which is a far better failure than a `KeyError` three nodes later. **The default branch still earns its place**, because provider-level constraint is not available everywhere and 4.7's distinction holds: a schema is a request to the provider, not a guarantee from the model.

nodes.label: Loud, and at the boundary
nodes.sub: not a KeyError three nodes later

nodes.label: The default branch still earns its place

d.title: Each thing it cannot do buys a property you can state
d.caption: The limits are the features. **It cannot call two handlers, so the number of paths equals the number of categories. It cannot loop or revisit a decision, so the model-call count is 1. It cannot sequence several operations, so maximum latency is classification plus the slowest handler** — a number you can write in a design document. And *can it run away?* **No, structurally** — not “unlikely”, not “bounded by a limit”.

nodes.label: A number for a design document
Can it run away? No, structurally

d.title: Two keys, and the counter is the one that is not a duplicate
d.caption: **A `current_tool` or `last_result` key is a duplicate: the message list already holds both, so you get two sources of truth that can disagree — and the message list is the one the model actually reads.** 8.8's tell applies as well: a key existing only so a router can read back what a node already knew is a `Command` waiting to happen. **The step counter is different** — it is a property of the run that no single node knows.

nodes.label: Two sources of truth that disagree
nodes.sub: and the model reads the list

nodes.label: The counter is not a duplicate

d.title: A model that never stops asking, and the graph returned anyway
d.caption: Three steps taken, then an `AIMessage` a caller can show a user — **the graph returned rather than raising.** Two things earn their place here. **The budget is in the router, so the graph exits instead of hitting the recursion limit** (8.9, 10.5). And `guarded` **wraps** `tools_condition` rather than replacing it — 9.2's unrolling done minimally: keep the prebuilt's logic, add the one thing it has no notion of.

d.title: Good at exploration, bad at commitment
d.caption: It fits when **the next action genuinely depends on the last result** — searching, diagnosing, following a trail, recovering from a tool failure by trying something else. It fits badly where a router already works, and badly on **long plans, because the model re-decides from scratch every turn and so has no commitment to a strategy.** And the cost is unpredictable for a plain reason: **the step count is model output.**

nodes.label: Exploration: search, diagnose, trail
nodes.sub: the next step depends on the last

nodes.label: Predictable cost
nodes.sub: the step count is model output

d.title: The critique feeds back into the next generation
d.caption: Three rounds, and the loop exits on the critic's `GOOD` rather than on a counter. What makes this a pattern and not just two prompts is the **feedback edge**: round 2's generator sees *“Too terse. State the payment method”*, so the critique is an **input** to the next draft rather than a report about the last one. Which is also where the cost comes from — §02 — because that text is carried forward.

state: Too terse. State the payment method.

d.title: Six calls is the floor, and the tokens are worse than six times
d.caption: **Each generation carries the previous critique and each critique carries the full draft, so the per-call token count grows with the round number — the sixth call is the most expensive one, not an equal sixth of the total.** Which means the honest way to price reflection is in **tokens rather than calls**, and that the growth is superlinear in rounds: *“just add one more round”* is not a sixth more cost.

nodes.label: So per-call tokens grow with the round
nodes.sub: the sixth call is the dearest

nodes.label: Price it in tokens, not calls

d.title: The first revision added the most, for a structural reason
d.caption: Round 1 to 2 adds the payment method; round 2 to 3 adds a processing time. **The diminishing return is not a tuning artefact to be optimised away — it follows from the critic being the same model with a different prompt, so it shares the generator's blind spots: a third round finds style issues because the errors it can see, it already saw.** Which is why a *different* model as critic behaves differently.

d.title: Three exits, and the flag is the only signal the loop is working
d.caption: The third exit is 10.5's progress check: **a critic that says the same thing twice means the loop is not converging.** And recording **which** exit fired is not optional monitoring — *“good enough”* and *“ran out of rounds”* produce the same output, so **the output alone cannot distinguish them, and a loop whose budget is always the exit has no real exit condition.**

nodes.label: Budget always the exit = no exit condition
